To use the order, one adds *positional encodings* (sinusoidal, learned, or RoPE, 6.2) — and on graphs: the analogue is the problem of *positional/structural encodings*, at the heart of chapter 10 and of the Advanced GNN module (M2);
-   **MLP**: two layers with GELU, expansion ratio \~4 — this is where most of the parameters live (\~2/3);
-   **Cross-attention** (encoder–decoder models: the original transformer, T5): a second attention sub-block in the decoder takes its queries from the decoder states $Y$ and its keys and values from the encoder output $H$,
    $$
    \mathrm{CrossAtt}(Y, H) = \mathrm{softmax}\Big(\frac{(YW_Q)(HW_K)^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\Big)\, HW_V,
    $$
    one output row per target token and no mask on the source. In code it is `F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q_from_Y, k_from_H, v_from_H)`. The same operation injects a text prompt into an image diffusion model (9.4).
-   **Causal mask**: forbid $j > i$ for autoregression — exactly the factorization $\mathbb{P}(x) = \prod_t \mathbb{P}(x_t \mid x_{<t})$ of chapter 9 and of the causal language models of section 6.5.

### 6.5. Modern NLP: tokens, embeddings and pretraining objectives {#modern-nlp}

The official syllabus lists "modern natural language processing" and "embeddings". A transformer consumes vectors, not text: this section explains how a sentence becomes a sequence of vectors, and what a language model is trained to predict before any task-specific adaptation (chapter 7).

::: def
[Definition 6.3 — Subword tokenization by byte-pair encoding (BPE)]{.tag} Start from a vocabulary of characters (or bytes) and split every word of the training corpus into them, with an end-of-word marker `_`. Repeatedly count all pairs of adjacent symbols, weighted by word frequency, and merge the most frequent pair into a new symbol, until the vocabulary $\mathcal{V}$ reaches a chosen size $|\mathcal{V}|$ (about $3 \times 10^4$ to $2 \times 10^5$ in current models). A new text is tokenized by applying the learned merges in the same order. No word is ever out of vocabulary, frequent words become single tokens and rare words are split into reusable pieces.
:::

::: ex
[Example 6.4 — Five merges by hand]{.tag} Corpus: "low" ×5, "lower" ×2, "newest" ×6, "widest" ×3. The pairs `e s`, `s t` and `t _` each occur $6 + 3 = 9$ times, more than any other pair, so the first merges are `es`, then `est`, then `est_` (ties broken by order of appearance). Next come `l o` and `lo w`, with 7 occurrences each. After these five merges the unseen word "lowest" is encoded as two tokens, `low` and `est_`: the tokenizer has discovered a stem and a suffix from frequencies alone.
:::

::: def
[Definition 6.5 — Embedding matrix, static and contextual embeddings]{.tag} Each token $w \in \mathcal{V}$ is mapped to a row $E_w$ of a learned matrix $E \in \mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}| \times d}$; this is the product of the one-hot vector of $w$ with $E$, so the gradient touches only the rows of tokens present in the batch.

Many language models reuse $E$ at the output, computing the next-token logits as $E\,h$ (weight tying).

A **static embedding** gives one vector per word whatever its context. Word2vec's skip-gram with negative sampling learns it without labels; its loss, its gradient and its matrix-factorization reading are derived later, in [theorem 4.1 of the NLP module](../m1p2-nlp-text-mining/index.html#ch4) (Period 2); here it is only stated. With a center vector $v_w$, a context vector $u_c$ and $k$ negatives $n_i$ drawn in proportion to frequency$^{3/4}$, one minimizes
$$
\mathcal{L} = -\log\sigma(u_c^\top v_w) - \sum_{i=1}^{k}\log\sigma(-u_{n_i}^\top v_w).
$$
At the optimum, $u_c^\top v_w$ is the pointwise mutual information of $(w, c)$ minus $\log k$ (Levy & Goldberg, 2014): words that share contexts get similar vectors.

The output of a transformer layer is a **contextual embedding**: the vector of "bank" differs in "river bank" and in "bank account", because attention has mixed in the neighbouring tokens.
:::

::: def
[Definition 6.6 — Pretraining objectives]{.tag} A **causal** (autoregressive) language model factorizes
$$
\mathbb{P}(x_1, \dots, x_n) = \prod_t \mathbb{P}(x_t \mid x_{<t})
$$
and minimizes the average negative log-likelihood
$$
\mathcal{L} = -\frac1n\sum_t \log p_\theta(x_t \mid x_{<t}),
$$
using the causal mask of section 6.4; this is the decoder-only family (GPT and most current LLMs).

A **masked** language model (BERT, an encoder) hides about 15% of the tokens and predicts them from the context on both sides; its representations serve classification and retrieval. Encoder–decoder models (T5) reconstruct masked spans of the input. In each case the labels come from the text itself: this is self-supervised learning.

The quality of a causal model is reported as its **perplexity** $\exp(\mathcal{L})$.
:::

::: ex
[Example 6.7 — Perplexity by hand]{.tag} A model assigns probabilities $\tfrac12, \tfrac14, \tfrac18, \tfrac12$ to the four tokens of a sentence. Its loss, in nats, is
$$
\mathcal{L} = \tfrac14(\ln 2 + \ln 4 + \ln 8 + \ln 2) = \tfrac74\ln 2 \approx 1.21,
$$
and its perplexity is
$$
2^{7/4} \approx 3.4:
$$
at each step the model is as uncertain as a uniform choice among about 3.4 tokens.

A uniform model over a vocabulary of $50{,}000$ tokens has perplexity $50{,}000$.
:::

```python
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F
vocab, n = 50_000, 4                            # |V| tokens, n positions
logits = torch.randn(n, vocab)                  # one row of scores per position
targets = torch.randint(0, vocab, (n,))         # the next tokens
loss = F.cross_entropy(logits, targets)          # average NLL over positions
print(loss.item(), torch.exp(loss).item())       # loss in nats, perplexity
```

### 6.6. Transformers beyond text: the vision transformer (ViT) {#vit}

A transformer only needs a sequence of vectors. The vision transformer of Dosovitskiy et al. (2021) turns an image into such a sequence by cutting it into patches, and then uses the encoder of 6.4 unchanged, without the causal mask.

::: def
[Definition 6.8 — Vision transformer (ViT)]{.tag} For an image of size $H \times W$ with $C$ channels and a patch side $P$:

1.  **Patchify**: cut the image into $N = HW/P^2$ patches and flatten each into a vector of size $P^2C$.
2.  **Linear projection**: map each patch to $\mathbb{R}^d$ with one shared matrix $E \in \mathbb{R}^{P^2C \times d}$, the same for every patch.
3.  **[CLS] token**: prepend one learned vector, whose final state serves as the summary of the image.
4.  **Learned positions**: add a learned table of $N + 1$ positions (6.2), so that the model knows where each patch was.
5.  **Encoder and head**: apply a stack of bidirectional blocks (12 in ViT-B), then a linear classifier on the final [CLS] state.
:::

```python
import torch, torch.nn as nn

B, C, H, W, P, d = 8, 3, 224, 224, 16, 768
x = torch.randn(B, C, H, W)
patchify = nn.Conv2d(C, d, kernel_size=P, stride=P)      # = one shared linear map per patch
tok = patchify(x).flatten(2).transpose(1, 2)               # (B, 196, 768)
cls = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(1, 1, d))                   # [CLS] token
pos = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(1, 1 + tok.shape[1], d))    # learned positions
z = torch.cat([cls.expand(B, -1, -1), tok], 1) + pos       # (B, 197, 768): ready for the blocks
print(z.shape)
```

::: ex
[Example 6.9 — ViT-B/16 on the counter]{.tag} A $224 \times 224$ RGB image with $P = 16$ gives $N = 196$ patches of $16 \cdot 16 \cdot 3 = 768$ numbers, plus [CLS]: $n = 197$ tokens of width $d = 768$, through 12 blocks with 12 heads.

-   **Parameters**: about $12d^2 = 7.1$ M per block, hence about 86 M in all; the 12 encoder blocks of BERT-base have the same size.
-   **Compute per block**: the projections and the MLP cost $12 n d^2$ multiply–adds, the scores and their product with $V$ cost $2n^2d$.
-   **Total**: about $17.5 \times 10^9$ multiply–adds per image (the figure often quoted as "17.6 GFLOPs" counts multiply–adds). The $n^2$ term is only 4% of it at $n = 197$.

With $P = 8$ the image gives $n = 785$ tokens and the cost rises to about $78 \times 10^9$ multiply–adds: a smaller patch buys resolution with compute, and the quadratic term starts to count.
:::

::: note
[Inductive bias, and where ViT goes next]{.tag} A CNN builds locality and translation equivariance into its weights (ch. 4); a ViT has neither, apart from the patch grid, and must learn them from data. This is why ViT matches or beats ResNets only after pretraining on large datasets (ImageNet-21k, JFT-300M), and why Exercise 12 compares the two on MNIST. ViT is the image encoder of CLIP and of most vision-language models (Multimodal Generative AI module); DeiT and Swin are treated in [Advanced DL, ch. 4](../m1p2-advanced-deep-learning/index.html#ch4).
:::

## 7. Transfer learning and fine-tuning {#ch7}

Training "from scratch" has become the exception: the dominant practice consists in starting from a model pre-trained on immense corpora (ImageNet for vision, terabytes of text for LLMs) and adapting it. This chapter gives the framework and the vocabulary; the LLMs module (M2) applies it at scale.

### 7.1. The three adaptation regimes

-   **Frozen features / linear probing**: freeze the whole backbone, train a linear classifier (or a small head) on the pre-trained representations. A valuable diagnostic: feature quality is measured by the performance of a simple softmax on top (exercise 12, step (d)).
-   **Full fine-tuning**: retrain all the weights with a smaller step (typically 10 to 100× smaller than pre-training) — the risk of *catastrophic forgetting* (loss of pre-trained knowledge) is managed by a decaying step and few epochs.
-   **Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT)**: train only a small fraction of new parameters, the rest staying frozen — all the more relevant as models grow.

::: note
[Why it works]{.tag} The low layers learn quasi-universal features (chapter 4: edges and textures in vision; in a pretrained text transformer, parts of speech and local syntax, as the probing study of Tenney, Das & Pavlick, 2019, shows); task specificity lives in the high layers. The performance versus number of labeled domain examples curve shifts massively to the left — this is the most measurable practical benefit of modern deep learning.
:::

::: ex
[Worked example — linear probe, partial and full fine-tuning of a ResNet-18]{.tag} Adapt an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-18 (11.18 M weights without its 1000-class head) to a 10-class task. The new head has $512 \times 10 + 10 = 5{,}130$ weights.

| Regime | Trainable weights | The backward pass goes through | Learning rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| Linear probe | 5,130 (0.05%) | the head only | large (fresh head) |
| Partial: last stage + head | 8.40 M (75%) | `layer4` and the head | small for `layer4`, large for the head |
| Full fine-tuning | 11.18 M (100%) | the whole network | 10 to 100 × below pretraining |

-   **Partial fine-tuning is cheap in compute, not in parameters.** The last stage holds three quarters of the weights of a ResNet-18, but the backward pass stops there and the frozen stages store no activations.
-   **The domain decides.** On a target close to ImageNet with a few hundred labels per class, the probe often comes within a few points of full fine-tuning and barely overfits. The further the domain moves (medical images, sketches), the more of the high layers must be retrained.
-   **Run the probe first.** It is the floor that any fine-tuning must beat, and it measures the quality of the features (exercise 12, step (d)). Keep frozen BatchNorm layers in `eval()` mode, or their running statistics still move.
:::

```python
def set_regime(model, regime):          # a torchvision resnet18 whose model.fc = nn.Linear(512, 10)
    for p in model.parameters():
        p.requires_grad = (regime == "full")
    if regime == "partial":
        for p in model.layer4.parameters():
            p.requires_grad = True
    for p in model.fc.parameters():     # the new head is always trained
        p.requires_grad = True
    return sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters() if p.requires_grad)   # 5130 / 8398858 / 11181642
```

### 7.2. Domain adaptation, in a nutshell

When the target has *no* labels (labeled source domain → unlabeled target domain), domain adaptation aligns the distributions: adversarial (a discriminator tries to guess the domain from the features: they must become non-discriminative), or via distribution distances (MMD, Wasserstein distances — a preview: they are defined in the [Optimal Transport](../m1p2-optimal-transport/index.html) module and in [Graph ML 9.6](../m1p2-graph-ml/index.html#ch9)). The guiding idea: learn representations *invariant* to the domain but *discriminative* for the task.

### 7.3. LoRA: a mathematical sketch

::: def
[Definition 7.1 — LoRA (Hu et al., 2021)]{.tag} For a pre-trained matrix
$$
W_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{out}} \times d_{\mathrm{in}}},
$$
one freezes $W_0$ and learns a low-rank update:
$$
W = W_0 + \Delta W = W_0 + \frac{\alpha}{r}\, B A, \qquad B \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{out}} \times r},\ A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times d_{\mathrm{in}}},\ r \ll \min(d_{\mathrm{in}}, d_{\mathrm{out}}),
$$
with $B$ initialized to zero and $A$ Gaussian: $\Delta W = 0$ at the start, training departs exactly from the pre-trained model. $\alpha/r$ sets the effective scale of the update.
:::

::: note
[Why a low rank suffices]{.tag} The working hypothesis, backed by Aghajanyan et al. (ACL 2021), is that weight updates during adaptation have a low "intrinsic rank": $\Delta W$ is well approximated by a product $BA$ of small rank $r$ (4 to 64 in practice).

Let us count: adapting a $d \times d$ layer with $r = 8$ costs $2dr = 16d$ parameters instead of $d^2$ — for $d = 4096$, a factor of $d/16 = 256$.

Other benefits: a single $W_0$ kept in memory + per-task interchangeable $(A, B)$ pairs (instant swap); and for inference latency, one can merge $W = W_0 + BA$ at no extra cost. The generalizations (QLoRA: quantized backbone + LoRA) are covered in [the LLMs module (M2), section 4.3](../m2-large-language-models/index.html#peft).
:::

```python
import torch, torch.nn as nn

class LoRALinear(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, base: nn.Linear, r=8, alpha=16):
        super().__init__()
        self.base = base                       # W0 frozen
        for p in self.base.parameters(): p.requires_grad = False
        self.A = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(r, base.in_features) * 0.01)
        self.B = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(base.out_features, r))
        self.scale = alpha / r
    def forward(self, x):
        return self.base(x) + self.scale * (x @ self.A.T @ self.B.T)
# trainable params: r*(in+out) instead of in*out
```

## 8. Training in practice {#ch8}

A network that does not learn almost always has a mundane bug. This chapter is the diagnostic protocol we will apply in the labs, in the order in which it must be applied.

### 8.1. The training recipe, in order

1.  **Shape sanity check**: one forward pass without errors, the dimensions of every activation verified (rule of ch. 0: gradients have the shape of their variable).
2.  **Overfit a single batch**: 32 examples, train until the loss is $\approx 0$. If the model cannot do it, the bug is *structural* (data, loss, initialization, wild learning rate) — no point training longer. A model unable to memorize 32 examples is broken or too small; this is THE test that avoids weeks of silent error.
3.  **LR range test** (Smith, 2015): $\eta$ increasing geometrically from $10^{-7}$ to $10^{0}$, plot the loss: plateau → descent → divergence. Take the $\eta$ at the dip (or slightly before): it sets AdamW/SGD in one epoch.
4.  **Small full training run** on \~10% of the data, with the train/val curves: check that the dynamics are healthy before scaling up.
5.  **Scaling + regularization**: larger batch (or gradient accumulation), mixed precision, data augmentation, dropout, weight decay — in that order of payoff (ch. 3).
6.  **Checkpointing**: save regularly (weights + optimizer state + current step + data generator seed), to resume exactly.

### 8.2. Monitoring: reading your curves

  Symptom                          Likely cause                                                       Response
  -------------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------ -------------------------------------------------------
  loss = NaN                       lr too large, log(0), unprotected softmax (ch. 0), fp16 overflow   divide lr by 10, log-softmax, loss scaling
  one-off loss spikes              aberrant batch, lr near the edge of 2/L (thm. 3.1)                 inspect the data, lower the lr, gradient clipping
  exploding gradient norm          poorly conditioned recurrences (ch. 5)                             clip $\|\hat g\|$ to a threshold (standard: 1.0)
  train goes down, val stagnates   overfitting                                                        ch. 3.6, in order of payoff
  neither train nor val moves      lr too small, blockage (dead ReLUs), loss mis-wired                LR range test, per-layer activation statistics

Tools: tensorboard/wandb; systematically log the loss, accuracy, gradient norm, weight norm, the fraction of zero activations (dying ReLU), and the activation histograms of a few layers.

### 8.3. GPU: the levers that matter

-   **Mixed precision** (bf16 preferably): \~2× throughput, memory divided by \~2 — the first reflex (ch. 2).
-   **Batch and accumulation**: saturate the GPU (measure utilization); if memory runs out, accumulate small batches; adjust the BatchNorm statistics accordingly.
-   **DataLoader**: workers > 0, pin_memory, prefetch — a GPU waiting for data is a wasted GPU (CPU preprocessing is often the real bottleneck).
-   **torch.compile**, fused kernels (FlashAttention, ch. 6), avoid CPU→GPU synchronizations inside the loop (the .item() / prints at each step).

The loop below puts the first and last of these levers together with experiment tracking. Autocast runs the matrix products in 16 bits and keeps reductions in float32; the gradient scaler is needed only for float16, whose narrow exponent range lets small gradients underflow (ch. 2.2). It runs as is on a CPU, in bfloat16.

```python
import torch, torch.nn as nn
from torch.utils.tensorboard import SummaryWriter        # pip install tensorboard

device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(32, 256), nn.GELU(), nn.Linear(256, 10)).to(device)
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=3e-4, weight_decay=1e-2)
use_fp16 = device == "cuda" and not torch.cuda.is_bf16_supported()  # old GPUs: fp16
dtype = torch.float16 if use_fp16 else torch.bfloat16
scaler = torch.amp.GradScaler(device, enabled=use_fp16)  # loss scaling, needed for fp16 only
writer = SummaryWriter("runs/exp1")                      # then: tensorboard --logdir runs

for step in range(100):
    x = torch.randn(64, 32, device=device)
    y = torch.randint(0, 10, (64,), device=device)
    with torch.autocast(device_type=device, dtype=dtype):  # matmuls in 16 bits, reductions in fp32
        loss = nn.functional.cross_entropy(model(x), y)
    opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
    scaler.scale(loss).backward()          # multiply the loss so that small fp16 gradients survive
    scaler.unscale_(opt)                   # true gradients again, before clipping
    gnorm = nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)
    scaler.step(opt)                       # skips the step if an inf or NaN appeared
    scaler.update()
    if step % 10 == 0:                     # .item() waits for the GPU: log every k steps only
        writer.add_scalar("train/loss", loss.item(), step)
        writer.add_scalar("train/grad_norm", gnorm.item(), step)
writer.close()
```

### 8.4. Reproducibility

```python
import torch, numpy as np, random

def seed_everything(seed=42):
    random.seed(seed); np.random.seed(seed); torch.manual_seed(seed)
    torch.cuda.manual_seed_all(seed)

seed_everything(42)
torch.backends.cudnn.deterministic = True    # determinism (speed cost)
torch.backends.cudnn.benchmark = False       # disable non-deterministic autotuning
```

Set the seeds (python/numpy/torch/cuda), the data shuffling, and record the library versions; some CUDA kernels remain non-deterministic by nature (atomics); aim for reproducibility *up to a tolerance* rather than bit-for-bit, and document configurations and seeds in every experiment. Reproducibility is also a debugging tool: a random bug you know how to reproduce is half fixed.

## 9. Generative models: AE, VAE, GAN {#ch9}

The networks of the previous chapters predict a label $y$ from an input $x$; a generative model learns the distribution of $x$ itself, so that it can produce new images or sentences. This chapter compares three ways of doing so — autoencoders, variational autoencoders and generative adversarial networks — and derives the training objective of each.

### 9.1. Deterministic autoencoder and its pathology

An autoencoder compresses $x$ into a code $z = E_\phi(x)$ and reconstructs $\hat x = D_\theta(z)$, trained on $\|x - \hat x\|^2$. Useful for representation learning though it is, it is not a *generative* model: the latent space has no imposed structure — sampling $z$ at random gives aberrant reconstructions. The VAE corrects precisely this.

::: note
[Linear autoencoder and PCA (Baldi & Hornik, 1989)]{.tag} Take centred data, a linear encoder $z = W_e x$ with $W_e \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times d}$, a linear decoder $\hat x = W_d z$ and the squared reconstruction error.

The map $x \mapsto W_d W_e x$ has rank at most $k$, so by the Eckart–Young theorem the best achievable error is that of the projection onto the top $k$ principal directions, and every global minimizer reconstructs through exactly that projection (when $\lambda_k > \lambda_{k+1}$). The weights themselves are identified only up to an invertible $k \times k$ change of basis of the code.

A linear autoencoder is thus PCA (Machine Learning module, section 7.3) learned by gradient descent; nonlinear encoders and decoders extend dimensionality reduction to curved data, and a *denoising* autoencoder, which reconstructs $x$ from a corrupted copy, learns features that are robust to that corruption.
:::

### 9.2. VAE: the ELBO fully derived {#elbo}

Sections 9.2 and 9.3 are the site's reference derivations of the ELBO and of the GAN equilibrium: the Multimodal Generative AI module and others recall them and link here.

::: def
[Definition 9.1 — VAE (Kingma & Welling, 2013)]{.tag} Diagonal Gaussian encoder
$$
q_\phi(z \mid x) = \mathcal{N}\big(\mu_\phi(x), \mathrm{diag}(\sigma_\phi^2(x))\big),
$$
decoder $p_\theta(x \mid z)$, prior $z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$. One maximizes the **ELBO** (evidence lower bound):
$$
\mathrm{ELBO}(\theta, \phi; x) = \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi}\big[\log p_\theta(x \mid z)\big] - \mathrm{KL}\big(q_\phi(z \mid x)\,\|\,\mathcal{N}(0, I)\big),
$$
that is, one minimizes the training loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{VAE}} = -\mathrm{ELBO}$, averaged over the data.
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 9.2 — Exact decomposition of the log-likelihood]{.tag} $$\log p_\theta(x) = \mathrm{ELBO}(\theta, \phi; x) + \mathrm{KL}\big(q_\phi(z\mid x)\,\big\|\,p_\theta(z \mid x)\big) \;\ge\; \mathrm{ELBO}(\theta, \phi; x).$$ Maximizing the ELBO = maximizing a lower bound of $\log p_\theta(x)$ *and* bringing $q_\phi(z \mid x)$ closer to the exact posterior $p_\theta(z \mid x)$.
:::

::: proof
Start from the definition of the KL between $q_\phi(\cdot \mid x)$ and the posterior $p_\theta(\cdot \mid x)$, both over $z$ (at fixed $x$), and expand with $p_\theta(x, z) = p_\theta(x \mid z)\, p(z)$ (Bayes):
$$
\mathrm{KL}\big(q_\phi \| p_\theta(\cdot \mid x)\big) = \mathbb{E}_q[\log q] - \mathbb{E}_q[\log p_\theta(x \mid z)] - \mathbb{E}_q[\log p(z)] + \log p_\theta(x).
$$
Now, by definition of the KL against the prior,
$$
\mathbb{E}_q[\log q] - \mathbb{E}_q[\log p(z)] = \mathrm{KL}(q_\phi \| \mathcal{N}(0,I)).
$$
Substituting:
$$
\mathrm{KL}\big(q_\phi \| p_\theta(\cdot \mid x)\big) = \mathrm{KL}(q_\phi \| \mathcal{N}) - \mathbb{E}_q[\log p_\theta(x \mid z)] + \log p_\theta(x),
$$
that is, rearranging:
$$
\log p_\theta(x) = \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_q[\log p_\theta(x \mid z)] - \mathrm{KL}(q_\phi \| \mathcal{N})}_{=\ \mathrm{ELBO}(\theta,\phi;x)} + \mathrm{KL}\big(q_\phi \| p_\theta(\cdot \mid x)\big).
$$
The KL is nonnegative (Jensen applied to $\mathbb{E}_q[\log(q/p)] \ge -\log \mathbb{E}_q[p/q] = 0$), giving the bound. Equality iff $q_\phi(z \mid x) = p_\theta(z \mid x)$ exactly. [∎]{.qed}
:::

::: note
[Reading the proof]{.tag} One cannot optimize $\log p_\theta(x) = \log \int p_\theta(x \mid z)\, p(z)\, dz$ directly: the integral is intractable. The ELBO is the only quantity that requires only (i) *samples* from $q_\phi$ (Monte Carlo: a single one suffices in practice) and (ii) a *closed-form* KL. It is the same trade-off as in EM (Machine Learning module): the residual KL measures exactly what the bound loses.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 9.3 — Reparameterization: why $z = \mu + \sigma \odot \varepsilon$ works]{.tag} If $\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$ and $z = \mu_\phi(x) + \sigma_\phi(x) \odot \varepsilon$, then
$$
z \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_\phi(x), \mathrm{diag}(\sigma_\phi^2(x)))
$$
*and*
$$
\nabla_\phi \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi}[f(z)] = \mathbb{E}_\varepsilon\big[\nabla_\phi f(\mu_\phi + \sigma_\phi \odot \varepsilon)\big]:
$$
the gradient gets through. Sampling $z \sim q_\phi$ directly blocks the gradient (the sampling operation has no derivative with respect to its parameters).
:::

::: proof
The law of $z$ is obtained by an affine change of variable, whose Jacobian
$$
\partial z/\partial \varepsilon = \mathrm{diag}(\sigma)
$$
is constant: the density of $z$ is that of a Gaussian with mean $\mu$, covariance $\mathrm{diag}(\sigma^2)$.

For the gradient: the expectation under $q_\phi$ rewrites as an expectation under the *fixed* law of $\varepsilon$,
$$
\mathbb{E}_{q_\phi}[f(z)] = \mathbb{E}_{\varepsilon}[f(\mu_\phi + \sigma_\phi \odot \varepsilon)];
$$
the distribution is *no longer* parameterized by $\phi$ — $\phi$ now appears only in the integrand, which gradient descent knows how to differentiate (theorem 2.1). [∎]{.qed}
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 9.4 — Closed-form KL between diagonal Gaussians]{.tag} For $q = \mathcal{N}(\mu, \mathrm{diag}(\sigma^2))$ and $p = \mathcal{N}(0, I)$ in dimension $k$: $$\mathrm{KL}(q \| p) = \frac12 \sum_{i=1}^{k} \big(\mu_i^2 + \sigma_i^2 - 1 - \log \sigma_i^2\big).$$
:::

::: proof
$\mathrm{KL}(q\|p) = \mathbb{E}_q[\log q(z) - \log p(z)]$. Coordinate by coordinate (the densities factorize), with $\varphi$ the standard Gaussian density:
$$
\log q(z_i) - \log \varphi(z_i) = -\tfrac12\log\sigma_i^2 - \frac{(z_i - \mu_i)^2}{2\sigma_i^2} + \frac{z_i^2}{2}.
$$
Under $q$, $z_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_i, \sigma_i^2)$, so $\mathbb{E}_q[(z_i - \mu_i)^2] = \sigma_i^2$ and $\mathbb{E}_q[z_i^2] = \mu_i^2 + \sigma_i^2$. Taking the expectation:
$$
-\tfrac12\log\sigma_i^2 - \tfrac12 + \tfrac12(\mu_i^2 + \sigma_i^2),
$$
that is $\tfrac12(\mu_i^2 + \sigma_i^2 - 1 - \log \sigma_i^2)$.

Along the way one checks that each term is $\ge 0$, zero iff $\mu_i = 0, \sigma_i = 1$ (study of $u - 1 - \log u \ge 0$). [∎]{.qed}
:::

::: note
[The ELBO trade-off in practice]{.tag} First term: reconstruction. Second: a regularizer that keeps the codes close to the prior — too strong, everything blurs together (codes ignored, blurry sampling); too weak, the latent space develops "holes" (partial posterior collapse). The connection with variational inference and EM is taken up again in the Machine Learning module; the extensions ($\beta$-VAE, VQ-VAE) are in Multimodal Generative AI.
:::

### 9.3. GAN: the minimax game and its equilibrium {#gan-equilibrium}

::: def
[Definition 9.5 — GAN (Goodfellow et al., 2014)]{.tag} Minimax game between a generator $G$ (often $G(z)$ with $z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$) and a discriminator $D : \mathcal{X} \to (0,1)$: $$\min_G \max_D \ V(G, D), \qquad V(G, D) = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_{\mathrm{data}}}\big[\log D(x)\big] + \mathbb{E}_{z \sim p(z)}\big[\log(1 - D(G(z)))\big].$$
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 9.6 — Optimal discriminator and global equilibrium]{.tag}

1.  For fixed $G$, the maximand reads (with $p_G$ the law of $G(z)$)
    $$
    V(G,D) = \int \big[p_{\mathrm{data}}(x)\log D(x) + p_G(x) \log(1 - D(x))\big] dx,
    $$
    maximized pointwise at
    $$
    D^\star(x) = \frac{p_{\mathrm{data}}(x)}{p_{\mathrm{data}}(x) + p_G(x)}.
    $$
2.  The value of the game is then
    $$
    V(G, D^\star) = -\log 4 + 2\,\mathrm{JSD}(p_{\mathrm{data}} \| p_G),
    $$
    minimized over $G$ exactly when $p_G = p_{\mathrm{data}}$: the global equilibrium exists and coincides with the law of the data.
:::

::: proof
**1)** For each fixed $x$, maximize $a\log D + b\log(1-D)$ with $a = p_{\mathrm{data}}(x)$, $b = p_G(x)$.

The derivative $a/D - b/(1-D) = 0$ gives $D^\star = a/(a+b)$ (strict concavity in $D \in (0,1)$).

**2)** Rewrite
$$
\log D^\star = \log \frac{p_{\mathrm{data}}}{p_{\mathrm{data}}+p_G} = \log\frac{p_{\mathrm{data}}}{m} - \log 2
$$
and
$$
\log(1 - D^\star) = \log \frac{p_G}{m} - \log 2,
$$
where $m = \frac12(p_{\mathrm{data}} + p_G)$. Then
$$
V(G, D^\star) = \int p_{\mathrm{data}} \log\frac{p_{\mathrm{data}}}{m} + \int p_G \log\frac{p_G}{m} - 2\log 2 = 2\,\mathrm{JSD}(p_{\mathrm{data}} \| p_G) - \log 4,
$$
by definition of the Jensen–Shannon divergence (average of the KLs toward $m$).

Since $\mathrm{JSD} \ge 0$ with equality if and only if $p_{\mathrm{data}} = p_G$ almost everywhere (each KL toward the mixture $m$ vanishes only when the law equals $m$), the minimum $-\log 4$ is reached exactly at equilibrium.

**Gaussian case**: if $p_{\mathrm{data}} = \mathcal{N}(\mu_d, \sigma_d^2)$ and $G(z) = \mu + \sigma z$, then $p_G = \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$ and the equilibrium corresponds to the exact parameters $(\mu, \sigma) = (\mu_d, \sigma_d)$.

The logit of $D^\star$, $\log p_{\mathrm{data}} - \log p_G$, is a degree-2 polynomial in $x$ — a quadratic discriminator suffices. [∎]{.qed}
:::

::: note
[Why it is unstable nonetheless]{.tag} The theorem describes the equilibrium, not the *dynamics*: the two players descend their gradients *simultaneously*, and if $D$ becomes too good too fast, the gradient of $G$ vanishes ($\log(1 - D)$ saturates). Emblematic pathology: **mode collapse** — $G$ concentrates on the "easiest" modes of $p_{\mathrm{data}}$ (a few very credible faces instead of all of them).

Historical remedies: Wasserstein-GAN (transportation distance instead of JSD — a preview: the distance is defined in the [Optimal Transport](../m1p2-optimal-transport/index.html) module and [Graph ML 9.6](../m1p2-graph-ml/index.html#ch9)), gradient penalization, feature matching. In imaging, the family was superseded by **diffusion** (iterative denoising): section 9.4 gives its loss and sampler, Ye Zhu's models (chapter 10) are recent developments of it, and the Multimodal Generative AI module treats them in detail.

LLMs, for their part, remain autoregressive: $\mathbb{P}(x_t \mid x_{<t})$, cross-entropy loss over tokens (LLMs module, M2).
:::

| Family | Principle | Sampling | In the program |
|---|---|---|---|
| VAE | ELBO, Gaussian latent | decoder from $z \sim \mathcal{N}$ | Multimodal GenAI |
| GAN | adversarial min-max | implicit | Multimodal GenAI |
| Diffusion | iterative noising/denoising | (reverse) process | 9.4 (self-study); Multimodal GenAI |
| Autoregressive | modeling $\mathbb{P}(x_t \mid x_{<t})$ | token by token | LLMs (M2), Graph GenAI |

### 9.4. Diffusion in one section (self-study) {#diffusion}

A VAE samples in one decoder pass but blurs; a GAN is sharp but unstable. Diffusion models (Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015; Ho, Jain & Abbeel, 2020) take a third route: a fixed process turns data into noise in many small Gaussian steps, and a network learns to undo one step at a time, with a plain regression as its loss.

This section gives the formulas that the rest of the program uses: discrete diffusion on graphs ([Graph ML 9.5](../m1p2-graph-ml/index.html#ch9)), [Geometric Data ch. 7–8](../m2-geometric-deep-learning/index.html#ch7) and [Advanced DL 10.4](../m1p2-advanced-deep-learning/index.html#ch10).

::: def
[Definition 9.7 — Forward (noising) process]{.tag} Choose a schedule $0 < \beta_1 < \dots < \beta_T < 1$ (Ho et al.: linear from $10^{-4}$ to $0.02$, with $T = 1000$), and set
$$
\alpha_t = 1 - \beta_t, \qquad \bar\alpha_t = \prod_{s=1}^{t} \alpha_s .
$$
The forward chain adds a little Gaussian noise at each step:
$$
q(x_t \mid x_{t-1}) = \mathcal{N}\big(\sqrt{\alpha_t}\, x_{t-1},\ \beta_t I\big).
$$
Step $t = 0$ is the data. At $t = T$, $\bar\alpha_T \approx 0$ and $x_T$ is almost pure noise.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 9.8 — Closed form at any step]{.tag} For every $t$,
$$
q(x_t \mid x_0) = \mathcal{N}\big(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\, x_0,\ (1 - \bar\alpha_t)\, I\big), \qquad\text{that is}\qquad x_t = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\, x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_t}\; \varepsilon, \quad \varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I).
$$
Training can therefore draw any step $t$ directly, without running the chain.
:::

::: proof
By induction on $t$, with $\bar\alpha_0 = 1$. Assume
$$
x_{t-1} = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\, x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_{t-1}}\, \varepsilon'.
$$
Then
$$
x_t = \sqrt{\alpha_t}\, x_{t-1} + \sqrt{\beta_t}\, \varepsilon_t = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\, x_0 + \Big(\sqrt{\alpha_t(1 - \bar\alpha_{t-1})}\, \varepsilon' + \sqrt{\beta_t}\, \varepsilon_t\Big).
$$
The bracket is a sum of two independent centred Gaussians, whose variances add up to
$$
\alpha_t(1 - \bar\alpha_{t-1}) + 1 - \alpha_t = 1 - \bar\alpha_t.
$$
[∎]{.qed}
:::

**From the ELBO to a regression.** The reverse model is a Gaussian chain started from $p(x_T) = \mathcal{N}(0, I)$:
$$
p_\theta(x_{t-1} \mid x_t) = \mathcal{N}\big(\mu_\theta(x_t, t),\ \sigma_t^2 I\big).
$$
Treating $x_{1:T}$ as the latent variables of a VAE, theorem 9.2 gives $\log p_\theta(x_0) \ge \mathrm{ELBO}$, and the negative ELBO splits into one term per step:
$$
-\mathrm{ELBO} = L_T + \sum_{t=2}^{T} L_{t-1} + L_0, \qquad L_{t-1} = \mathbb{E}_q\, \mathrm{KL}\big(q(x_{t-1} \mid x_t, x_0)\,\big\|\,p_\theta(x_{t-1} \mid x_t)\big).
$$
$L_T$ has no parameter, since the prior is fixed, and $L_0$ is a decoder term.

::: prop
[Proposition 9.9 — The ε-prediction loss (Ho et al., 2020)]{.tag} By Bayes' rule on Gaussians, the forward posterior $q(x_{t-1} \mid x_t, x_0)$ is Gaussian with variance $\tilde\beta_t I$ and mean $\tilde\mu_t$:
$$
\tilde\beta_t = \frac{1 - \bar\alpha_{t-1}}{1 - \bar\alpha_t}\,\beta_t, \qquad \tilde\mu_t = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}\Big(x_t - \frac{\beta_t}{\sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_t}}\, \varepsilon\Big),
$$
where $x_0$ was replaced by its expression from proposition 9.8. Give the reverse mean the same form, with a network $\varepsilon_\theta(x_t, t)$ in place of the unknown $\varepsilon$. Then, up to a constant $C_t$ free of $\theta$,
$$
L_{t-1} = \frac{\beta_t^2}{2\sigma_t^2\, \alpha_t\, (1 - \bar\alpha_t)}\; \mathbb{E}\,\big\|\varepsilon - \varepsilon_\theta(x_t, t)\big\|^2 + C_t .
$$
:::

::: proof
The KL between two Gaussians with covariances $\tilde\beta_t I$ and $\sigma_t^2 I$ is $\|\tilde\mu_t - \mu_\theta\|^2 / (2\sigma_t^2)$ plus a term that depends on the variances only. The two means differ only through the noise:
$$
\tilde\mu_t - \mu_\theta = \frac{\beta_t}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}\,\sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_t}}\,\big(\varepsilon_\theta(x_t, t) - \varepsilon\big),
$$
and squaring gives the weight. [∎]{.qed}
:::

::: key
[Key result — the diffusion training loss]{.tag}
$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{simple}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t,\, x_0,\, \varepsilon}\, \Big\| \varepsilon - \varepsilon_\theta\big(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\, x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_t}\, \varepsilon,\ t\big) \Big\|^2, \qquad t \sim \mathcal{U}\{1, \dots, T\}.
$$
:::

Ho et al. drop the weight of proposition 9.9: the samples get better, at the price of a looser bound.

::: thm
[Algorithm 9.10 — Ancestral sampling]{.tag} Draw $x_T \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$. For $t = T, \dots, 1$, draw $z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$ (and set $z = 0$ at the last step), then
$$
x_{t-1} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}\Big(x_t - \frac{\beta_t}{\sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_t}}\, \varepsilon_\theta(x_t, t)\Big) + \sigma_t z, \qquad \sigma_t^2 = \beta_t \ \text{ or } \ \tilde\beta_t .
$$
Output $x_0$. A sample costs $T$ network evaluations, against one for a VAE or a GAN; DDIM and distillation cut this number ([Multimodal GenAI, ch. 4](../m1p2-multimodal-genai/index.html#ch4)).
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 9.11 — Predicting the noise is estimating the score]{.tag} Let $p_t$ be the law of $x_t$. The best predictor in $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{simple}}$ is the conditional mean
$$
\varepsilon^\star(x, t) = \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon \mid x_t = x],
$$
and
$$
\nabla_x \log p_t(x) = -\frac{\varepsilon^\star(x, t)}{\sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_t}} .
$$
A trained $\varepsilon_\theta$ is thus an estimate of the *score* $\nabla \log p_t$, which links DDPM to score-based models and Langevin sampling (Song et al., 2021).
:::

::: proof
The minimizer of a squared error is the conditional expectation. Next, $p_t(x) = \int q(x \mid x_0)\, p(x_0)\, dx_0$; differentiating under the integral,
$$
\nabla p_t(x) = \int q(x \mid x_0)\, \nabla_x \log q(x \mid x_0)\; p(x_0)\, dx_0 .
$$
Dividing by $p_t(x)$ and using Bayes' rule, $\nabla \log p_t(x)$ is the conditional mean of $\nabla_x \log q(x \mid x_0)$ given $x_t = x$. By proposition 9.8,
$$
\nabla_x \log q(x \mid x_0) = -\frac{x - \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\, x_0}{1 - \bar\alpha_t} = -\frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_t}},
$$
and taking the conditional mean ends the proof. [∎]{.qed}
:::

**Classifier-free guidance** (Ho & Salimans, 2022). To condition on a prompt $c$ (a class, a caption), train one network $\varepsilon_\theta(x_t, t, c)$ and replace $c$ by an empty token $\varnothing$ on about 10% of the examples. At sampling time, extrapolate from the unconditional prediction toward the conditional one:
$$
\tilde\varepsilon_w = \varepsilon_\theta(x_t, \varnothing) + w\,\big(\varepsilon_\theta(x_t, c) - \varepsilon_\theta(x_t, \varnothing)\big).
$$
With $w = 1$ this is the plain conditional model; $w > 1$ over-guides, giving samples more faithful to the prompt and less diverse. By proposition 9.11, it samples with the score
$$
\nabla \log p_t(x) + w\, \nabla \log p_t(c \mid x).
$$
This is the site's convention for the guidance weight ([notation page](../../notation/index.html#diffusion)); the original paper writes $w' = w - 1$.

The toy below trains $\varepsilon_\theta$ on a mixture of eight Gaussians in the plane and samples with algorithm 9.10. It runs on a CPU in under a minute.

```python
import math, torch, torch.nn as nn

torch.manual_seed(0)
def data(m):                                          # 8 Gaussians on a circle of radius 2
    k = torch.randint(0, 8, (m,)) * (math.pi / 4)
    return 2 * torch.stack([k.cos(), k.sin()], 1) + 0.1 * torch.randn(m, 2)

T = 100
beta = torch.linspace(1e-4, 0.2, T)                   # beta_1, ..., beta_T (index t - 1)
alpha, abar = 1 - beta, torch.cumprod(1 - beta, 0)    # abar_t = alpha_1 ... alpha_t
net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2 + 16, 256), nn.SiLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.SiLU(),
                    nn.Linear(256, 2))
def eps_theta(x, t):                                  # the step t enters as sin/cos features
    f = t.float().unsqueeze(1) / T * torch.arange(1, 9) * math.pi
    return net(torch.cat([x, f.sin(), f.cos()], 1))
opt = torch.optim.Adam(net.parameters(), lr=1e-3)

for step in range(5000):                              # training: regress the noise
    x0, t = data(256), torch.randint(0, T, (256,))
    eps = torch.randn_like(x0)
    xt = abar[t, None].sqrt() * x0 + (1 - abar[t, None]).sqrt() * eps   # prop. 9.8
    loss = ((eps - eps_theta(xt, t)) ** 2).mean()     # L_simple
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()

with torch.no_grad():                                 # ancestral sampling (algorithm 9.10)
    x = torch.randn(2000, 2)
    for t in reversed(range(T)):
        e = eps_theta(x, torch.full((2000,), t))
        x = (x - beta[t] / (1 - abar[t]).sqrt() * e) / alpha[t].sqrt()
        if t > 0:
            x = x + beta[t].sqrt() * torch.randn_like(x)   # sigma_t^2 = beta_t
ang = torch.arange(8) * (math.pi / 4)
dist = torch.cdist(x, 2 * torch.stack([ang.cos(), ang.sin()], 1)).min(1)
print(f"{(dist.values < 0.4).float().mean():.0%} of samples within 0.4 of a mode, "
      f"{dist.indices.unique().numel()} modes out of 8")   # about 90%, 8 modes
```

::: note
[Normalizing flows: an exact likelihood]{.tag} A flow is an invertible network $g_\theta$ that maps the data $x$ to a latent $z = g_\theta(x)$ of the same dimension, with $z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$. The change of variables gives the exact log-likelihood:
$$
\log p_\theta(x) = \log \mathcal{N}\big(g_\theta(x);\, 0, I\big) + \log \big|\det J_{g_\theta}(x)\big| .
$$

-   **Affine coupling** (RealNVP: Dinh, Sohl-Dickstein & Bengio, 2017). Split $x = (x_a, x_b)$, keep $x_a$, and transform $x_b$ with scales and shifts computed from $x_a$:
    $$
    z_a = x_a, \qquad z_b = x_b \odot \exp\big(s(x_a)\big) + t(x_a).
    $$
-   **Cheap determinant, explicit inverse.** The Jacobian is triangular, so its log-determinant is the sum of the entries of $s(x_a)$. The inverse is $x_b = (z_b - t(z_a)) \odot \exp(-s(z_a))$, and the networks $s$ and $t$ can be anything.
-   **Trade-off.** Stacking couplings that alternate the split gives a model trained by plain maximum likelihood, with no bound and no adversary. The price: the latent has the dimension of the data, and invertibility constrains the architecture.
:::

**From the VAE decoder to text-to-image.** Latent diffusion (Rombach et al., 2022) runs the whole process of this section in the latent space of a pretrained autoencoder trained with a light KL penalty, as in 9.2. A $512 \times 512 \times 3$ image becomes a $64 \times 64 \times 4$ latent, the denoiser works there, and the decoder maps the final latent back to pixels.

The prompt enters through the cross-attention of 6.4, with keys and values computed by a frozen text encoder (in Stable Diffusion, the public release of latent diffusion, the CLIP text encoder of Radford et al., 2021), and classifier-free guidance sets how strongly it is followed. The families of this chapter thus end up in one pipeline, built in full in the [Multimodal Generative AI](../m1p2-multimodal-genai/index.html) module.

## 10. Research at DaSciM (Vazirgiannis, Lutzeyer, Zhu) {#ch10}

This chapter connects the course to the current research of three researchers of the DaSciM group: Michalis Vazirgiannis (responsible of the course on the sheet), Johannes Lutzeyer (in its teaching team) and Ye Zhu (not listed on the 2026–2027 sheet). All three topics are rooted in the previous chapters. The arXiv references are in the bibliography.

### 10.1. Michalis Vazirgiannis: from the "Graph of Words" to textual GNNs

::: ex
[Worked example — Graph of Words (Rousseau & Vazirgiannis, CIKM 2013)]{.tag} The *bag-of-words* representation throws away syntactic and order structure; the **word graph** restores it at almost no cost:

-   **Construction**: each distinct term of the document = one node; a *sliding window* of size $w$ over the text creates an edge between two terms if they co-occur in the window (weighted by the co-occurrence frequency). The document becomes a small, sparse weighted graph.
-   **From TF-IDF to TW-IDF**: in a bag of words, the weight of a term is its frequency; in a word graph, it is its *centrality*. TW-IDF weights the term by its in-degree in that document's own graph-of-words (the unweighted version worked best), with a pivoted normalization by document length, times the usual collection-level IDF. The group then used the k-core decomposition of the word graph for keyword extraction (Rousseau, Kiagias & Vazirgiannis, ECIR 2015). "Ad hoc" retrieval gains over TF-IDF: structurally important words emerge even when they are rare.
-   **Positioning with respect to the course**: this is the first building block of the program — *the data itself becomes a graph*. The NLP module reuses these representations; the Graph ML module generalizes them.
:::

::: note
[GNN lineage: texts, expressivity, generation]{.tag}

-   **One graph per document** (MPAD: Nikolentzos, Tixier & Vazirgiannis, AAAI 2020): each *document* is its own word graph, read by a message-passing network with attention. A new document is processed without rebuilding anything, whereas TextGCN (Yao et al., AAAI 2019) built a single transductive corpus graph. TextING (Zhang et al., ACL 2020) applies the same per-document idea to inductive text classification.
-   **DGoW-GNN** (Abbahaddou, Lutzeyer & Vazirgiannis, NeurIPS 2023): *discriminative* word graphs — the edges are no longer fixed co-occurrences but are filtered/learned for the task, then a GNN propagates the representations. The loop is closed with chapter 2: the computation graph (backprop) and the data graph (message passing) answer each other.
-   **PathNN** (Michel, Nikolentzos & Vazirgiannis, ICML 2023): going beyond classical message passing by aggregating *paths* (shortest paths, simple paths) emanating from each node; two variants are strictly more expressive than the Weisfeiler–Lehman test. This is the language of the Graph ML module, expanded in Advanced GNN (M2).
:::

### 10.2. Johannes Lutzeyer: where are the parameters? Expressivity and position

::: note
[Sparsifying the update step (Lutzeyer, Wu & Vazirgiannis, 2021)]{.tag} An MPNN (message passing neural network) chains two phases: the aggregation of neighbor messages and an "update step" — precisely the linear transformation + non-linearity of chapter 1, applied node by node. The paper's question: what remains if one *sparsifies* this trainable step, initializing it directly sparse (ExpanderGNN, with a tunable sparsity rate) or even reducing it to a non-linearity alone (Activation-Only GNN)?

Key result: performance comparable to dense models with far fewer parameters — a direct empirical insight into how expressivity is distributed between aggregation (structure, not parametrized) and the update (parametrized), in the spirit of ch. 1 (what, in a network, carries the expressivity?).
:::

::: note
[Positional encodings on graphs (SHAKE-GNN, Cui, Lutzeyer et al., 2025)]{.tag} Chapter 6 showed that a transformer needs a positional *encoding* because, without positions, self-attention is permutation-equivariant: permuting the tokens only permutes the outputs, so the order is lost (invariance only comes after a symmetric pooling).

On a graph, the problem is deeper: there is *no canonical ordering* of the nodes — the "position" of a node is a *structural* notion (Laplacian spectrum, distances, spanning forests). SHAKE-GNN proposes hierarchical encodings based on Kirchhoff forests, computed in a scalable way. The parallel to remember: RoPE (relative absolute position, suited to sequences) vs spectral/structural encodings (position defined by the geometry of the graph); both answer the same fundamental symmetry (exercise 4). The Advanced GNN module (M2) systematizes this question.
:::

### 10.3. Ye Zhu: steering diffusion models

::: note
[From the loss to semantic control]{.tag} Section 9.4 gives the loss, the sampler and the guidance of diffusion models; the work of Ye Zhu shows how to *steer* them further:

-   **BoundaryDiffusion** (Zhu et al., NeurIPS 2023): control the semantics of generation *without retraining* (learning-free), by warping the decision boundaries of the model's latent space in the guidance plane — an elegant point of contact with theorem 9.6: where the GAN sought an equilibrium, here already-learned latent regions are moved geometrically.
-   **Discrete contrastive diffusion** (ICLR 2023) and **Diffusion in Diffusion** (ICLR 2024): *discrete* cross-modal music-image diffusion and cyclic text-vision conditioning — the argument of the ch. 9 table ("multimodal") made concrete.
-   **NoiseQuery** (ICCV 2025): the initial noise $z_T$ as an *implicit control signal* for goal-guided generation — it reverses the perspective: the "noise" becomes a structured input, which connects to the sensitivity to the initial noise studied for GANs/diffusion.

This work directly extends ch. 9 and is expanded in the Multimodal Generative AI module.
:::

## Exercises {#ex}

1.  **★ Backprop on paper.** Redo example 2.2 by hand (a scalar tanh network). Then write the backward pass of a two-layer ReLU network with the recursion of theorem 2.1, and check it numerically, as in the NumPy code of section 2.1, by central finite differences
    $$
    \frac{\mathcal{L}(\theta + \epsilon e_j) - \mathcal{L}(\theta - \epsilon e_j)}{2\epsilon}
    $$
    on a small network.
2.  **★ Activation.** Show that if $\sigma$ is linear, an MLP of arbitrary depth represents exactly the affine maps. Deduce why *linear cascades* are useless.
3.  **★ 1D attention by hand.** For $n = 3$ tokens, $d_k = 2$, compute by hand $QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k}$, the row-wise softmax, and the result $\mathrm{softmax}(\cdot)V$. Implement it, compare, and check that the rows of the attention matrix sum to 1.
4.  **★ Permutation-equivariance.** Take the block of 6.4 with `causal=False`, in `eval()` mode and without positional encoding. Check experimentally that permuting the tokens permutes the output rows in the same way (equivariance), that the mean over the tokens is then invariant, and that adding a positional encoding breaks both properties. The proof is proposition 4.4 of [Advanced DL](../m1p2-advanced-deep-learning/index.html#ch4).
5.  **★ Quadratic SGD.** Take $A = \mathrm{diag}(4, 1)$, $b = 0$, $\theta_0 = (1, 1)$.

    Write the sequence $(\theta_k)$ for $\eta = 1/2$ then $\eta = 1$, and verify theorem 3.1 (per-mode contraction, bound $2/L$).
6.  **★ Convolution arithmetic.** A $32 \times 32$ input, three successive convs (5×5, stride 2, padding 2; 3×3, stride 1, padding 1; 3×3, stride 1, padding 1, dilation 2): intermediate output sizes and final receptive field (proposition 4.4).
7.  **★ LoRA.** Count the trainable parameters of a GPT-like model with 12 blocks ($d = 768$, attention + MLP) adapted by LoRA $r = 8$ on the attention projections only, and compare with full fine-tuning.
8.  **★★ He initialization.** Recover the factor 2 of He initialization: for $h = \mathrm{ReLU}(a)$ with $a$ symmetric zero-mean, compute $\mathbb{E}[h^2]$ then the variance of the next layer.
9.  **★★ Adam bias correction.** Prove proposition 3.5 for $v_t$ (second moment), then compute the update $\hat m_1/\sqrt{\hat v_1}$ at the first step and explain why the warmup protects.
10. **★★ Gaussian KL.** Derive the formula of proposition 9.4 in dimension 1, plot
    $$
    \mathrm{KL}(\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2) \| \mathcal{N}(0,1))
    $$
    as a function of $\mu$ and $\sigma$, and locate the minimum.
11. **★★ Gaussian GAN.** For $p_{\mathrm{data}} = \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ and $p_G = \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$, write the logit of $D^\star$ (difference of the log-densities) and check that it is a trinomial in $x$. Where does the equilibrium lie?
12. **★★★ Project.** In PyTorch: classify MNIST with (a) an MLP, (b) a small CNN, (c) a mini-transformer on patches (16 patches of 7×7, a 4 × 4 grid, as in the ViT of 6.6). Plot the train/val curves, compare the parameter counts and accuracy, comment with the bias-variance decomposition, then apply the protocol of chapter 8 (overfitting a batch, LR range test). (d) Train the CNN of (b) on the digits 0–4, freeze it, and train a linear classifier on its features for the digits 5–9 (linear probing, section 7.1); compare with the CNN trained from scratch on 5–9.

::: note
[Solutions (Ex. 2, 3, 5, 6, 11) and hints (the others)]{.tag}

-   **Ex. 1.** Take $\epsilon \sim 10^{-6}$ in float64 for the check; the error of the central finite difference is $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^2)$. In float32, rounding swamps such a small $\epsilon$ (section 2.2).
-   **Ex. 2.** By induction: if
    $$
    h^{(\ell)} = \sigma(W^{(\ell)} h^{(\ell-1)} + b^{(\ell)})
    $$
    with $\sigma(t) = \alpha t$, then
    $$
    h^{(\ell)} = \alpha W^{(\ell)} h^{(\ell-1)} + \alpha b^{(\ell)}
    $$
    remains affine in $h^{(0)} = x$ — composing, $f_\theta(x) = W x + c$ with $W = \prod_\ell \alpha W^{(\ell)}$: a single matrix, all the deep layers collapse into one.
-   **Ex. 3.** The row-wise softmax makes each row a vector of positive weights of sum 1; the multiplication by $V$ makes each output a weighted average of the *values*: this is a convex interpolation, exactly the message passing of chapter 6.
-   **Ex. 4.** Permute the *token* dimension, `x[:, perm]`; `x[perm]` would permute whole sequences of the batch, a trivial check. Without the mask the property is exact up to rounding: the softmax over the keys is unchanged by re-indexing, and LayerNorm and the MLP act token by token. With the causal mask, token $i$ sees only the tokens $j \le i$, and the check fails. Dropout must be off.
-   **Ex. 5.** Decoupled modes: $(\theta_k)_1 = (1 - 4\eta)^k$, $(\theta_k)_2 = (1-\eta)^k$.

    For $\eta = 1/2$: factors $-1$ (oscillation without decay: exactly $\eta = 2/L$, limiting case) and $1/2$.

    For $\eta = 1$: factors $-3$ (divergence: $\eta > 2/L$) and $0$ (convergence in one step: $\eta = 1/\lambda_2$).
-   **Ex. 6.** Theorem 4.2: $32 \to 16 \to 16 \to 14$ (the third one: $\lfloor (16 + 2 - 2\cdot 2 - 1)/1 \rfloor + 1 = 14$).

    Receptive field (proposition 4.4, with dilation: replace $(k-1)$ by $d(k-1)$): $\mathrm{RF}_1 = 5$, $\mathrm{RF}_2 = 5 + 2 \cdot 2 = 9$, $\mathrm{RF}_3 = 9 + (2 \cdot 2)\cdot 2 = 17$ pixels, for a product of strides $\prod s = 2$.
-   **Ex. 7.** Per block: 4 attention matrices $d \times d$, i.e. $4 \times 2 \times 8 \times 768 = 49{,}152$ LoRA parameters, versus $4 \times 768^2 \approx 2.36$ M for full — and the MLP is not adapted; LoRA total \~0.6 M for \~85 M full.
-   **Ex. 8.** By symmetry of $a$,
    $$
    \mathbb{E}[h^2] = \mathbb{E}[a^2 \mathbf{1}_{a>0}] = \tfrac12\mathbb{E}[a^2]:
    $$
    the variance of the next layer is halved, hence $\mathrm{Var}(W) = 2/n_{\mathrm{in}}$.
-   **Ex. 9.** Re-derive the geometric sum with $g_k^2$ constant; at step 1, $\hat m_1 = g_1$ and $\hat v_1 = g_1^2$.

    The ratio is $\mathrm{sign}(g_1)$, a step of size $\eta$ whether $g_1$ is tiny or huge: hence the caution of the warmup when $g_1$ is atypical.
-   **Ex. 10.** The minimum of $\tfrac12(\mu^2 + \sigma^2 - 1 - \log\sigma^2)$ is reached at $\mu = 0$, $\sigma = 1$ (derivative with respect to $\sigma^2$: $\tfrac12(1 - 1/\sigma^2) = 0$).
-   **Ex. 11.** Unique global minimum at $(\mu, \sigma) = (0, 1)$; the logit of $D^\star$ is
    $$
    \frac{x^2}{2}\big(\frac{1}{\sigma^2} - 1\big) - \frac{x\mu}{\sigma^2} + \frac{\mu^2}{2\sigma^2} + \log\sigma:
    $$
    a trinomial in $x$, identically zero at the equilibrium $(\mu, \sigma) = (0, 1)$.
:::

## Projects and assessment {#projects}

The SynapseS sheet gives the grade format (numeric out of 20, with a US letter grade), but "the section for the LLGA track is empty": no assessment form, resit rule, pass threshold or ECTS is displayed for LLGA, and no breakdown of assessments is given for any degree. The subjects, the exam and the rubric below are therefore proposals of these notes, for instance half project and half written exam. They exercise objectives O1 (ML and DL foundations), O2 (generative modelling) and O3 (large language models), with O7 (hands-on practice) throughout.

Group projects 1 and 3 are the Deep Learning building blocks of two [Year 1 end-of-year projects](../../projects/index.html#year1) of the Graph × LLM route: a GraphRAG question-answering system ([Y1.1](../../projects/index.html#y1-1)) and the generation of molecules from text ([Y1.4](../../projects/index.html#y1-4)).

### Solo projects {#projects-solo}

1.  **[Solo · ≈ 20 h] Backprop from scratch and an initialization study.** Does a hand-written backward pass match autograd, and which initializations keep the signal alive through depth?
    -   *Implement*: extend the NumPy MLP of 2.1 to any depth and to sigmoid, tanh, ReLU and GELU, and check it against PyTorch autograd and a float64 central-difference checker. Measure activation and gradient variances layer by layer in a 20-layer network for zero, Xavier and He initializations (1.3), and reproduce XOR (example 1.4).
    -   *Data*: synthetic Gaussian inputs, XOR, and MNIST (LeCun et al., 1998).
    -   *Deliverables*: code with tests, a 4-page report with one variance-versus-depth plot per activation, a 10-minute talk.
    -   *Chapters*: ch. 0, 1, 2.
    -   *Success*: a relative gradient error below $10^{-7}$ on every tensor. With width 256 and ReLU, He keeps the activation variance after 20 layers within a factor 2 of the input, while Xavier divides it by about $2^{20} \approx 10^6$, as proposition 1.6 predicts.
2.  **[Solo · ≈ 25 h] Paper study: decoupled weight decay (Loshchilov & Hutter, ICLR 2019).** Is Adam with an L2 penalty really worse than AdamW, and does the best weight decay depend less on the learning rate once decoupled?
    -   *Warm-up*: check theorem 3.1 and proposition 3.3 on quadratics with $\kappa \in \{10, 100, 1000\}$. The number of iterations to reach an error of $10^{-6}$ should grow like $\kappa$ for gradient descent and like $\sqrt\kappa$ for tuned momentum.
    -   *Implement*: train a ResNet-20 (He et al., 2016) on CIFAR-10 (Krizhevsky, 2009) with Adam + L2 and with AdamW, over a 4 × 4 grid of learning rates and weight decays, with warmup and a cosine schedule (3.4). A 30-epoch run takes a few minutes on a free GPU tier.
    -   *Paper*: I. Loshchilov, F. Hutter, *Decoupled Weight Decay Regularization*, ICLR 2019 (its figures 1 and 2: test error over a grid of learning rates and weight decays).
    -   *Deliverables*: code, the two heatmaps, a 5-page report, a 10-minute talk.
    -   *Chapters*: ch. 3, 4, 8.
    -   *Success*: log-log slopes of 1 and 1/2 on the quadratics, within 10%; heatmaps that reproduce the paper's finding (a basin less tilted for AdamW), or a report that explains why not.

### Group projects {#projects-group}

1.  **[Group of 3 · ≈ 30 h each] Mini-GPT: tokenizer, pretraining and LoRA adaptation.** What does each ingredient of a small decoder-only transformer buy, and how close does LoRA come to full fine-tuning?
    -   *Implement*: a BPE tokenizer (definition 6.3); a pre-norm causal transformer with RoPE (6.2–6.4) of about 10 M parameters, pretrained on TinyStories (Eldan & Li, 2023); ablations of the $\sqrt{d_k}$ scaling and of pre- versus post-norm; then adaptation to SST-2 sentiment classification (Socher et al., 2013) by linear probe, LoRA with $r \in \{4, 8, 16\}$ and full fine-tuning (ch. 7).
    -   *Split*: member A builds the tokenizer, the data pipeline and the perplexity evaluation; member B the model, the pretraining and the ablations; member C the adaptation and the attention maps drawn as graphs (6.3).
    -   *Deliverables*: a repository, a 6-page report, a 15-minute talk.
    -   *Chapters*: ch. 6, 7, 8; it leads to [NLP, ch. 7](../m1p2-nlp-text-mining/index.html#ch7) and [Large Language Models, section 4.3](../m2-large-language-models/index.html#peft).
    -   *Success*: a validation perplexity far below that of a unigram model; LoRA with $r = 8$ within 2 points of full fine-tuning with under 2% of the weights trained, or an explanation of the gap.
2.  **[Group of 3 · ≈ 30 h each] Inductive biases on images: MLP, CNN, ViT and a graph network.** How much data does each architecture need, and what does each one build in? This extends exercise 12 and bridges to [Graph ML](../m1p2-graph-ml/index.html#ch5).
    -   *Implement*: on CIFAR-10, an MLP, a small ResNet (ch. 4), a ViT with 4 × 4 patches (6.6), and a GNN on SLIC superpixel graphs (Achanta et al., 2012). Train each on 1k, 5k and 50k images with the protocol of ch. 8, with tracked and seeded runs (8.4).
    -   *Paper*: the CIFAR10 superpixel benchmark of V. P. Dwivedi et al., *Benchmarking Graph Neural Networks*, JMLR 2023, whose GNN results the group reproduces for one model.
    -   *Split*: member A the MLP and the CNN; member B the ViT; member C the superpixel graphs and the GNN ([Graph ML, ch. 5](../m1p2-graph-ml/index.html#ch5)); shared training and logging code.
    -   *Deliverables*: a repository, a 6-page report, a 15-minute talk. *Chapters*: ch. 4, 6, 8, and Graph ML ch. 5.
    -   *Success*: a table of parameters, accuracy and data efficiency for the four models over three seeds; the reproduced GNN within the range reported by Dwivedi et al. for its size; a paragraph that explains the ranking at 1k images by the inductive biases of 4.1 and 6.6.
3.  **[Group of 2 · ≈ 25 h each] VAE, GAN and diffusion: theory checks and failure modes.** Do the generative families reach their theoretical optimum where it is known, and how do they fail?
    -   *Implement*: a linear autoencoder compared with PCA (9.1); a VAE with the reparameterization trick (9.2); a GAN on the eight-Gaussian ring and on MNIST, with the Gaussian check of theorem 9.6 and exercise 11; the diffusion toy of 9.4 on the same ring.
    -   *Split*: member A the autoencoders and the VAE (ELBO curves, posterior collapse); member B the GAN and diffusion (mode counts, samples, latent interpolations).
    -   *Data*: synthetic rings and MNIST. *Deliverables*: code, a 5-page report, a 10-minute talk.
    -   *Chapters*: ch. 9; it prepares the [Multimodal Generative AI](../m1p2-multimodal-genai/index.html) module.
    -   *Success*: principal angles between the autoencoder subspace and the PCA subspace below 1°; the number of ring modes covered by the GAN and by diffusion over five seeds; a fitted logit of $D^\star$ that matches the trinomial of exercise 11.

### Written exam (proposal) {#projects-exam}

Format: 2 hours, one handwritten A4 sheet allowed, no electronic device; four exercises, 20 points.

1.  **Question (5 points).** Scaled dot-product attention. (a) Write single-head attention for $n$ tokens of width $d$ and give its cost. (b) If the components of a query and a key are i.i.d., centred, with variance 1, show that their dot product has variance $d_k$, and say what goes wrong without the factor $1/\sqrt{d_k}$. (c) Without positions and without mask, show that self-attention is permutation-equivariant. How does one obtain an invariant output?

    *Expected*:

    -   **(a)** The formula of definition 6.1, with time $\mathcal{O}(n^2 d)$ and memory $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$ (1 point).
    -   **(b)** The proof of proposition 6.2; without the factor, the softmax saturates into a one-hot vector and its gradient vanishes (2 points).
    -   **(c)** For a permutation matrix $\Pi$, the scores become $\Pi QK^\top \Pi^\top$, the row softmax commutes with this re-indexing, and the output becomes $\Pi$ times the old one; a mean over the tokens is invariant (2 points).
2.  **Question (6 points).** Take
    $$
    f(w_1, w_2) = \tfrac12\big(w_2\,\mathrm{ReLU}(w_1 x) - t\big)^2, \qquad x = 2,\ w_1 = 0.5,\ w_2 = -1,\ t = 1.
    $$
    Then: (a) compute the forward values. (b) Compute both partial derivatives by backpropagation. (c) Take one gradient step with $\eta = 0.1$ and give the new loss. (d) A 3 × 3 convolution from 3 to 16 channels, stride 2, padding 1, reads a 64 × 64 image: give the output size and the number of parameters.

    *Expected*:

    -   **(a)** $a = w_1 x = 1$, $h = 1$, $y = -1$, loss 2 (1 point).
    -   **(b)** $\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial y = y - t = -2$, so $\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial w_2 = -2 \cdot h = -2$ and $\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial w_1 = (-2)(-1)(1)(2) = 4$ (2 points).
    -   **(c)** $w_1 = 0.1$ and $w_2 = -0.8$; the new loss is $\tfrac12(1.16)^2 = 0.6728$ (1.5 points).
    -   **(d)** Theorem 4.2 gives $\lfloor 63/2 \rfloor + 1 = 32$, so a $32 \times 32$ output, with $3 \cdot 9 \cdot 16 + 16 = 448$ parameters (1.5 points).
3.  **Question (5 points).** For a fixed generator of density $p_G$, (a) prove that the discriminator maximizing $V(G, D)$ is $D^\star = p_{\mathrm{data}}/(p_{\mathrm{data}} + p_G)$; (b) deduce
    $$
    V(G, D^\star) = -\log 4 + 2\,\mathrm{JSD}(p_{\mathrm{data}} \,\|\, p_G),
    $$
    and say for which $G$ the minimum is reached.

    *Expected*: (a) pointwise maximization of $a \log D + b \log(1 - D)$, concave, with zero derivative at $D = a/(a+b)$ (2 points). (b) Substitute, introduce the mixture $m = \tfrac12(p_{\mathrm{data}} + p_G)$ and recognize the two KLs toward $m$ (2 points); the JSD is non-negative and vanishes only when $p_G = p_{\mathrm{data}}$ (1 point).
4.  **Question (4 points).** Gradient descent on $f(\theta) = \tfrac12 \theta^\top A \theta$ with $A = \mathrm{diag}(10, 1)$. (a) For which step sizes does it converge from every start? (b) Give the best constant step and its rate. (c) About how many iterations divide the error by $10^3$?

    *Expected*: (a) $0 < \eta < 2/L = 0.2$ (1 point). (b) $\eta^\star = 2/(L + \mu) = 2/11 \approx 0.18$, rate $\rho = (\kappa - 1)/(\kappa + 1) = 9/11 \approx 0.82$, by theorem 3.1 (2 points). (c) $k \ge \ln 1000 / \ln(11/9) \approx 34.4$, so 35 iterations (1 point).

### Grading rubric (proposal) {#projects-rubric}

| Criterion | Weight | What earns the marks |
|---|---|---|
| Correctness and checks | 25 % | gradient checks and unit tests pass; numbers agree with the results of the chapters used |
| Experimental protocol | 20 % | baselines, several seeds with error bars, the recipe of ch. 8, tracked and reproducible runs |
| Analysis | 25 % | each result is explained by a proposition or theorem of the course; failures are diagnosed, not hidden |
| Report and figures | 15 % | 4–6 pages, plots with axes, units and legends, stated limitations |
| Talk and questions | 15 % | 10–15 minutes; every member can explain every part of the work |
